extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers, health researchers, journal editors and policy-makers concerned with publication and dissemination bias
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidence for identifying, understanding causes of, and judging the consequences of publication- and related dissemination-biases in health research (basic, observational, clinical) to inform systematic reviews and policy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome reporting bias exists and is likely to have important effects on pooled summary data within systematic reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited evidence indicates that harm and subjectively assessed outcomes may be more vulnerable to biased selective reporting than efficacy and objectively assessed outcomes. Reviewers should be alert to outcome-based selective reporting when extracting results for meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time lag bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies with significant or positive results tend, on average, to be published earlier than non-significant or negative studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One consequence can be a diminishing effect size reported by studies over time. Evidence is mixed and limited; reviewers should consider timing of publication when assessing pooled effects and look for unpublished or late-published negative studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grey literature bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Published studies tend to report a greater treatment effect than those of grey literature or unpublished studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction of bias is unpredictable for individual cases; grey literature studies may be small and of poor quality (but not always). Inclusion of grey literature can have important clinical implications and should be considered in systematic reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding non-English-language studies from systematic reviews may be associated with greater, similar or smaller estimates of treatment effects depending on field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heterogeneous impact across areas; exclusion appears to pose particularly high risk of bias in some fields such as complementary and alternative medicine. Reviewers should assess whether language restrictions could bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence indicates that studies with significant or positive results are on average associated with a higher frequency of citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-systematic narrative reviews are especially vulnerable to biased citation leading to misleading conclusions; systematic reviewers should use comprehensive search methods rather than relying on cited literature alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Covert duplicate publication of data may introduce bias in systematic reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although limited new evidence was identified, reviewers should seek to detect duplicate reporting (multiple publications from same data) to avoid double-counting and biased estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of publication / database / country / media attention biases
rubrics_metrics.description: There is still very limited evidence on place of publication bias, database or index bias, country bias and media attention bias, but these may exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of these potential biases; well-conducted systematic reviews can mitigate their impact through broad searching, inclusion of non-indexed sources and sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for patients and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication and related biases can lead to misleading estimates of treatment effects, resulting in avoidable suffering of patients and waste of limited resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include patients receiving harmful or ineffective treatments and increased costs from overestimated effects. Reviewers and policy-makers should consider potential bias when making clinical or funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators' reasons for non-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Main reasons investigators give for not publishing include lack of time or low priority, results not important enough, and journal rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pooled estimates: lack of time/low priority (~34.5%), results not important (~19.6%), journal rejection (~10.2%). 'Lack of time' may be used as an excuse for not publishing unimportant or non-significant results; surveys and pooled analyses support these as common drivers of non-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators' selective submission (submission bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative evidence shows that studies with significant/positive results are more likely to be submitted and submitted more rapidly than null/negative studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission bias may be a principal source of publication bias (submitted papers already skewed toward positive results). Reviewers should seek registered protocols and unpublished data to detect this source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators' delays due to intellectual property concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays to publication are sometimes reported due to patent application submission, protection of scientific lead, patent negotiation, or resolution of intellectual property ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys found these reasons commonly cited (e.g., patent application 46% among respondents reporting delays). These non-scientific incentives can postpone dissemination and contribute to time-lag bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' criteria for choosing journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors commonly consider journal prestige, readership makeup, whether the journal publishes on the topic, and likelihood of acceptance when choosing where to submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranked factors: journal prestige and readership are highly important; manuscript acceptance likelihood and subject fit drive initial and subsequent submissions. These selection behaviours can contribute to differential publication across topics and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial valuation: significance and importance over validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors primarily value the significance and importance of the research above validity of experimental and statistical methods; originality and clinical significance are also key criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative criteria include originality, predictability, triviality, narrow interest, specialisation, and clinical implications. Confirmatory studies and negative results may have lower acceptance chances; journal instructions that de-emphasise confirmations can foster bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence from journal owners may be limited; editors report pressures from association leadership and staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys showed variable editorial freedom; governance structures (board authority to hire/fire editors) suggest a need to protect editorial independence to reduce external pressures that could influence publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review — confirmatory / preconception bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers' preconceptions can bias assessments: referees judged sham papers less favourably when results conflicted with their own perspectives (confirmatory bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sham-paper experiments show poor inter-reviewer agreement and bias toward reviewers' prior views. Journals should be aware of confirmatory bias in peer review and consider procedures (blinding, diverse reviewer selection) to mitigate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review — quality bias and outcome neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor quality manuscripts are more likely to be rejected than good quality ones; some studies found no evidence of reviewer bias against positive or negative outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments indicate manuscript quality strongly affects acceptance; evidence on outcome-based reviewer bias is mixed. Peer review reforms should prioritise consistent quality assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract review unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing abstracts is less predictable and more likely to be biased than reviewing full articles, with low inter-reviewer agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conference abstract grading shows weak correlation between reviewers; reviewers and chairs should recognise limitations of abstract-only assessments and use caution in extrapolating from abstracts to published evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer source bias (author-nominated vs editor-selected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-nominated reviewers are significantly more likely to recommend acceptance and less likely to recommend rejection than editor-selected reviewers, though review quality and speed may be similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies comparing reviewer sources suggest nomination can increase favorable recommendations; journals should weigh potential bias when allowing author-nominated reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical bias in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical and language effects influence peer review: English-language versions and reviewer-author same-country pairings often receive more favorable ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments and retrospective analyses found English-language versions judged better, and greater acceptance/recommendation when reviewers and authors share country origin. Journals should consider strategies (language support, diverse reviewer pools) to reduce geographic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender-related patterns exist in peer review (e.g., female editors assigned female authors more often; mixed evidence on acceptance differentials), indicating potential for gender-related biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings are mixed across studies (some show differences in assignment/rejection patterns, others find no acceptance-rate differences). Editorial boards should monitor gender patterns in submission handling and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional prestige bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional prestige can influence referees' recommendations and editorial decisions, observed for brief reports but not necessarily for major papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective analyses show higher acceptance recommendations for manuscripts from prestigious institutions in some categories. Blind review systems and awareness can help reduce prestige-related bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of submitted manuscripts not strongly tied to result direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohort studies of submitted manuscripts found no significant association between acceptance and the direction or statistical significance of findings (pooled OR 1.06; 95% CI: 0.80 to 1.39).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests submission bias (selective non-submission) rather than editorial rejection based on results may be a primary driver of publication bias. Reviewers should therefore investigate submission practices and seek unpublished data when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cohorts of protocols/registered/submitted studies to detect bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that follow cohorts of research protocols, submitted or registered studies are less selective and provide more convincing evidence on publication and related biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evaluations of bias should prioritise cohort-based designs (protocol cohorts, trial registries, manuscript submission cohorts) to reduce selective reporting artefacts that affect retrospective case series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity and case-by-case assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings from individual empirical studies are often heterogeneous; pooled estimates may not be generalisable to many individual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A case-by-case approach is required to gauge the possible impact of publication and related biases and to decide appropriate measures to deal with these biases in a given review or policy decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-publication harms future research participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-publication of harmful findings can lead to repeated testing of harmful treatments on new patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cases (e.g., lorcainide) illustrate that withheld negative safety data led to further trials exposing patients to harm; full dissemination of negative and safety findings is ethically imperative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media coverage bias and misreporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Media coverage tends to favor positive or striking results and may fail to report basic study facts, potentially misleading the public; prominent news coverage of meeting abstracts is not predictive of formal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies found media articles often covered positive studies more and gave them longer coverage; media may misreport preliminary findings presented at meetings. Researchers and communicators should ensure accurate reporting of study limitations and publication status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of funding/conflicts influences media tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Media coverage of clinical trials can be influenced by disclosure of funding information and competing interests in the scientific and medical literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses showed media coverage of conflicts of interest affected overall article tone. Transparent disclosure in publications and press materials may influence how media portray study findings.
